title: Summer Catalog

jokes.text: Tom names Ron's raccoon hat 'Swiss Family Ron-binson' and says 'that hat is dope'
jokes.setup: Ron is wearing a raccoon-skin hat
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately riffs on 'Swiss Family Robinson' to name the hat, then seamlessly transitions to wanting to use it as a pickup prop
jokes.explanation: The 'Swiss Family Ron-binson' pun is quick and clever, perfectly in character for Tom's need to name and brand everything. The immediate pivot to wanting to borrow it for pickup lines establishes his entire arc for the cold open efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, what's with the hat? You look like you're about to join the Swiss Family Swanson!

jokes.text: Tom's increasingly desperate raccoon-hat pickup lines, culminating in 'Nice hat. Want to bone?' — attributed back to himself as coming from the woman
jokes.setup: Tom rehearses pickup lines using the raccoon hat as a gimmick to meet women
jokes.punchline: After several overwrought romantic lines, he pivots to the blunt 'Nice hat. Want to bone?' and frames it as the woman talking to him, then admits it didn't work
jokes.explanation: The escalating sequence of pickup lines — from raccoon metaphors to 'manimal in the bed' to pure bluntness — is a well-structured bit that captures Tom's delusion perfectly. The moment he frames 'Nice hat. Want to bone?' as the woman speaking TO him is a great self-aware beat. Pure Tom Haverford character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Can I try on your hat, Ron?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm gonna put this bad larry on my dome.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I mean, this hat on my head.

jokes.text: 'You know what they say — Animal on the head, Manimal in the bed.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying on romantic/sexy pickup lines using the raccoon hat
jokes.punchline: He invents a fake folk saying that rhymes 'animal' with 'manimal' as a self-aggrandizing boast
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable and very specifically Tom — the fake folk wisdom structure ('you know what they say'), the invented portmanteau 'manimal,' the absurd confidence. Short, punchy, and totally in character. One of the episode's best pure one-liners.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey ladies, check out this hat. It's made from the pelt of an animal that Ron killed with his bare hands.

jokes.text: 'Damn, girl, your hotness killed my raccoon.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying increasingly absurd pickup lines
jokes.punchline: He delivers a surreal compliment suggesting the woman's attractiveness has literally killed the stuffed raccoon on his head
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent absurdist line. The economy is near-perfect — seven words, completely ridiculous premise delivered with total sincerity, and it works as both a pickup line and as a character beat. Highly quotable. Comparable in quality to a polished comedy writer's room gem. Just shy of the 8.0 anchor but earns the score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know, that raccoon hat really brings out your eyes. We actually have a lot in common, you and that raccoon.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You both dig through trash.

jokes.text: 'I have a raccoon hat. I'm an interesting person.' — Tom's dejected final attempt
jokes.setup: Tom's elaborate pickup routines have all failed
jokes.punchline: He strips away all the wordplay and just states the premise baldly, as if raw sincerity might work where creativity failed
jokes.explanation: The deflation from elaborate wordplay to this pitiable stripped-down statement is perfectly structured. The comedy comes from recognizing the pathetic logic — having exhausted all his material, Tom thinks earnestness is somehow a fresh approach. Strong character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey baby, are you a raccoon? Because you're trash— wait, no, that's not... that came out wrong.

jokes.text: Tom's raccoon pickup line: 'Are you a raccoon? Because you've been running around my hat all da— head all day.'
jokes.setup: Tom is riffing on the raccoon-hat premise to deliver a pickup line riff on 'running through my mind all day'
jokes.punchline: He starts to say 'hat' (the raccoon's domain) then self-corrects to 'head' — fumbling the recovery of an already bad pun
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: a corny pickup line pun AND Tom fumbling the delivery by accidentally saying the wrong word. The meta-failure of the pickup attempt adds a layer. Competent and funny for this type of comedic cold open.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget everything I just said. I'm just gonna be honest. You are incredibly beautiful, and I would very much like to take you to dinner.

jokes.text: 'Damn, girl, your hotness killed my raccoon.'
jokes.setup: Tom is using the raccoon hat as a pickup prop
jokes.punchline: He claims a woman's attractiveness was so powerful it killed the raccoon on his head — a compliment framed as a complaint about property damage
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly imaginative pickup line. The logic is absurd (hotness = raccoon killer) but there's genuine creativity in the construction. Tom treating the hat as a sentient victim of female beauty is delightfully weird.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey baby, are you duck season? Because I want to blast you with my shotgun.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, that doesn't even make sense.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, it's rabbit season then. Same thing.

jokes.text: Ron's surprise birthday party story: he saw friends hiding, drove to a gas station, called the cops, and reported a break-in at his own home
jokes.setup: Leslie says she has a surprise for Ron; Ron says he's not big on surprises
jokes.punchline: He explains his response to a previous surprise party — not fleeing, but actively calling the police to arrest his own friends
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's strongest joke. It perfectly distills Ron Swanson's character: extreme privacy, tactical thinking, distrust of emotional gestures, and complete willingness to weaponize bureaucratic systems against his own social circle. The escalation from 'not big on surprises' to 'I called the cops on my friends' is perfectly calibrated. It's earned entirely through character, not shock. Rivals the 8.0 anchor and approaches the 9.5 territory — held back only slightly because it's a single anecdote rather than a sustained comedic structure.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You gotta have a motto. Mine is: 'If you really wanna get the hoochie, you gotta pay the price to get the smoochie.' It's like Manimal, but about gettin' ladies.

jokes.text: 'Think of the September issue of Vogue, but it's more important to Pawnee, mainly because we don't get Vogue here.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is hyping up the summer parks catalog as a major publication
jokes.punchline: She undercuts her own grandiose comparison by revealing Pawnee doesn't even receive Vogue — which makes the catalog important by default, not merit
jokes.explanation: Beautifully constructed Leslie joke — she starts with an overreach comparison, then self-corrects in a way that makes things worse. The joke works on two levels: it mocks Pawnee's smallness and illustrates Leslie's earnest inability to see how her 'correction' deflates her own point. Pure Leslie Knope character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Your beauty is so blinding, it killed my hat.

jokes.text: 'Centerfold? Always the best part. Am I right, Justin?' — then the documentary crew cuts to reveal Justin is Ann's ex who dumped her six weeks ago
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions moving an ad to the centerfold; Tom enthusiastically agrees and appeals to Justin for validation
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Justin is the man who broke Ann's heart six weeks ago — making Tom's casual appeal to male solidarity awkward
jokes.explanation: Functional expository joke that introduces Justin's awkward presence in the office. The comedic payoff — 'You broke up six weeks ago' — is mild situational irony rather than a crafted punchline. Gets the job done setting up future awkwardness.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I own a raccoon hat. I'm interesting.

jokes.text: Morgan the pedophile is in the softball photo — 'We had dinner together.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Jerry for softball pictures for the catalog; the group notices something wrong with one
jokes.punchline: The man in the photo is identified as a registered sex offender, and Jerry defends his presence by saying they had dinner together
jokes.explanation: The dark punchline lands on Jerry's naive obliviousness — he had dinner with a pedophile and found him 'okay.' Effectively dark without being gratuitous, and perfectly in character for hapless Jerry. April's follow-up is what elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's it. I'm done. This hat is cursed. I'm throwing it away.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: Wait! I love that hat. Where did you get it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You... you like it?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: Are you kidding? It's amazing. Can I have your number?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Of course! Finally!

jokes.text: 'Can you photoshop your life with better decisions, Jerry?'
jokes.setup: Tom suggests photoshopping the sex offender's face out of the photo
jokes.punchline: April pivots from the photoshop suggestion to a withering existential attack on Jerry's life choices
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. The structure is perfect: Tom sets up the photoshop solution, April hijacks the exact same verb to deliver a devastating existential insult at Jerry. The economy is exceptional — it's a complete character assassination in one sentence. Highly quotable. April's deadpan cruelty here is at its finest. Fully justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't like surprises. They're inefficient, they're unpredictable, and they often involve people screaming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But Ron, we just want to do something nice for you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The last surprise party I attended ended with me calling the police on my own friends and filing a restraining order against the host.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head confessional: 'I tivo through shows to get to the ads. I love ads.'
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining his expertise in advertising for the catalog
jokes.punchline: He admits he skips the actual content of TV to watch advertisements — the exact opposite of normal behavior, delivered as a point of pride
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Tom's consumerist, brand-obsessed identity taken to its logical extreme. The escalation from 'I love magazine ads' to 'I TiVo through shows to get to the ads' is structured beautifully — each step more absurd, delivered with total earnestness. Pure character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This parks catalog is as important as Vogue magazine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We don't get Vogue.

jokes.text: April's photo pitch: existential nihilist images with captions like 'Are we alone? Is the real winter inside our hearts?'
jokes.setup: Tom asks for one perfect, captivating image for the summer catalog cover
jokes.punchline: April presents a series of bleak, pretentious fine-art photographs with pseudo-philosophical captions — for a municipal parks summer catalog
jokes.explanation: Classic April — she takes the assignment completely seriously by her own standards while being completely wrong for the brief. The gap between 'summer parks catalog' and 'philosophical meditation on existential isolation' is maximally funny. The specific captions ('Is the real winter inside our hearts?') are well-written absurdist comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm putting myself in the next parks catalog. Full centerfold. Really sell the department.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'll call it 'Parks and Rec-reation.' Get it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Justin? Justin, buddy? No? Nothing?

jokes.text: Leslie's three-point critique of April's pitch: wrong season, complete gibberish, child looks abandoned — 'So basically, boo.'
jokes.setup: April has just presented an extremely pretentious, depressing photo concept
jokes.punchline: Leslie dismantles it methodically and then summarizes her entire critique with the single word 'boo' — a cheerfully bureaucratic rejection
jokes.explanation: The structure — numbered bureaucratic critique followed by a childish 'boo' — is a great Leslie Knope comedy beat. She's simultaneously the most organized and most charmingly dorky character, and this line captures both. The economy of 'basically, boo' as a summary is very good.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He's not going to respond to you. He doesn't know who you are. You're not in his phone. You're not in his life. You're a stranger to him.

jokes.text: Tom accidentally includes a personal photo in the slideshow — the reaction as the group sees something clearly inappropriate or embarrassing
jokes.setup: Tom is cycling through catalog photo options for the group
jokes.punchline: A personal photo appears — Tom stumbles over excuses ('It must've...') while the group reacts; then someone casually suggests it could work as the cover
jokes.explanation: Standard embarrassing-photo gag; the humor relies heavily on the actual image we can't see. The secondary beat — someone suggesting it could work as the cover — extends it well. Functional cringe comedy without being especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey, who is this guy? He looks familiar... Oh wait, isn't that Jerry Gergich's cousin? No, that's the guy from the sex offender registry.

jokes.text: Ann surprises Ben(Mark) with a six-month anniversary gift — a chicken salad sandwich; he produces a Swiss Army watch saying 'Swiss Army watch, mofo'
jokes.setup: Ann gives Mark a chicken salad sandwich for their anniversary and preemptively tells him not to feel bad about not getting her anything
jokes.punchline: He pulls out an expensive Swiss Army watch and says 'Swiss Army watch, mofo' — completely undercutting her gracious lowering of expectations
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection structure — Ann sets up the emotional let-down direction, Mark surprises with something good, then undercuts the sweetness by saying 'mofo.' The word 'mofo' as punctuation on a sweet romantic gesture is a nice tonal subversion.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, I had dinner with him last week, so...

jokes.text: 'Are you allowed to kiss me in a hospital room?' / 'Oh, don't worry about it. He's dead.' / 'Oh, my god.' / 'I'm just kidding. He's sleeping.'
jokes.setup: Mark and Ann share a moment in the hospital; Mark is reassured about kissing in the room
jokes.punchline: Ann nonchalantly says the patient is dead, then immediately walks it back — 'just kidding, he's sleeping' — leaving Mark (and the audience) briefly horrified
jokes.explanation: Well-structured dark misdirect — the casual delivery of 'he's dead' is the joke, and the quick correction deflates the horror perfectly. The capper 'that guy really seemed dead' in the confessional is a nice button. Good structural use of the talking-head format.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I can photoshop his face out of the picture.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Or you could photoshop your entire life out instead.

jokes.text: Mark's talking head: 'That guy really seemed dead.'
jokes.setup: Ann just revealed she was joking about the patient being dead
jokes.punchline: Mark's lingering uncertainty — stated flatly in confessional — suggests he's still not entirely convinced
jokes.explanation: A solid button on the previous joke. The callback adds a small grace note without overstaying its welcome. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: The parks catalog should reflect the duality of nature and civilization. It's about the liminal space between order and chaos, where the soul finds its true reflection in the mirror of existence.

jokes.text: Food fight with smoked salmon — 'April threw the smoked salmon on the roof.'
jokes.setup: The group is inventorying picnic supplies; Leslie asks about the smoked salmon
jokes.punchline: April threw it on the roof. No explanation, no apology beyond a flat 'I'm sorry.'
jokes.explanation: Pure April — she did something inexplicable and petty and offers only a flat, clearly insincere apology. The unexplained motivation is the joke. Economy is excellent: three words deliver the whole absurd scenario.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What is the sound of one hand clapping? What is the sound of one person not caring? Because that's me. I'm that person.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If a tree falls in the forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound? If I leave this meeting early, does anyone notice I'm gone? Probably not.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We are all just floating through an infinite void of meaninglessness, searching for purpose in a purposeless universe. Also, I need everyone to sign these expense reports.

jokes.text: Leslie texts the group from someone else's phone pretending to be them — 'She just texted me from your phone and said she left her phone at home and that I should come here immediately, and why did I believe that?'
jokes.setup: Mark asks where Leslie is; Tom reveals she orchestrated the group's arrival through an absurdly convoluted text scheme
jokes.punchline: Mark's self-aware 'and why did I believe that?' — acknowledging he was manipulated by a transparent Leslie scheme
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie-character beat — her schemes are always slightly too elaborate and transparent, yet people go along with them. Mark's self-aware question is the laugh. Competent but not especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I love the concept, I really do, but the lighting is all wrong, your posture is terrible, and honestly, the whole vibe is just... basically, boo.

jokes.text: Leslie suggests the universe guided Tom to come: 'Maybe in your heart you knew it was from me, but you came anyway.' / Mark: 'Nope.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to frame Mark's compliance with her text scheme as somehow romantic or intuitive
jokes.punchline: Mark's flat, immediate 'Nope' deflates any sentimentality entirely
jokes.explanation: The single-word deflation is perfectly timed. Leslie's earnest overreach versus Mark's complete unwillingness to play along captures their dynamic well. Economy score is high because 'Nope' is doing a lot of comic work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! That's not—that's a personal photo!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Can we just skip past that? Nobody needs to see that.

jokes.text: Tom suggests the couples should 'go on more dates with Tom.' Ann agrees: 'You have, and thank god an opportunity presented itself.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to justify why Ann and Mark should do the photo shoot — framing it as a date that includes him
jokes.punchline: He confirms Ann has genuinely said they should go on dates with Tom, implying it's a recurring delusional statement he takes seriously; Mark's sarcastic 'thank god' signals how unwelcome this is
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat establishing Tom's obliviousness and his odd presence as a third wheel. The joke is in Mark's resigned sarcasm. Not particularly crafted but serves its purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? Forget about the embarrassment. We should use that photo for the cover. It's perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: People connect with vulnerability. It's authentic. It's raw. It shows I'm real.

jokes.text: Tom asks Ann 'And would it kill you to put on some lipstick? Do you even own lipstick?' while directing the photo shoot
jokes.setup: Tom is directing Ann and Mark for the catalog photo shoot and gives fashion notes
jokes.punchline: He asks if she even owns lipstick — implying she's so naturally beautiful she never needs makeup, which reads as both a backhanded compliment and genuine cluelessness
jokes.explanation: Tom's casual presumptuousness as a self-appointed director is funny, but the joke is relatively mild. It works better as character setup for the later photo shoot disaster than as a standalone beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, is this a normal-sized cup, or is it a really big cup?

jokes.text: 'Sweater swap. She noticed. You were right.' — the old directors caught in the middle of trading sweaters
jokes.setup: Leslie is about to introduce the former parks directors; someone notices something odd
jokes.punchline: Two old men are mid-sweater-swap and are caught — one confirms the other predicted someone would notice
jokes.explanation: Delightful absurd detail — why are old men swapping sweaters? The economy of the exchange ('She noticed. You were right.') implies an entire backstory. The visual gag works even in transcript because the dialogue tells us exactly what's happening. Charming and weird.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I got you something special for our anniversary.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's a sandwich.

jokes.text: 'I thought you were dead, Clarence.' / 'No, I'm gonna outlive you, then I'm gonna nail your wife.'
jokes.setup: The four former parks directors are assembled; one expresses surprise another is still alive
jokes.punchline: Clarence responds not with relief or warmth but with a threat to outlive his rival and sleep with his wife
jokes.explanation: Exceptional dark comedy. The setup ('I thought you were dead') invites sympathy or relief; the punchline weaponizes that softness into something shockingly hostile. The specificity ('nail your wife') and the calm, matter-of-fact delivery implied by the context makes it devastating. Economy is near-perfect. The audience's laugh would be a mix of shock and delight. Fully earns the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Happy anniversary! I got you a sandwich.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: A sandwich? Ann, that's... actually really thoughtful. I got you something too.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: It's a weekend trip to the spa. We're gonna get massages, facials, the whole thing.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Mark, that's amazing! I can't believe you did this.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: That's what I'm talking about. We out here living our best life, you feel me? This anniversary is straight fire.

jokes.text: 'Classic David. You're worse than Ron.' / 'Shut your damn mouth, Tansley.'
jokes.setup: The old men immediately begin sniping at each other at their reunion
jokes.punchline: Leslie tries to play it off as charming ('Classic David') while being compared unfavorably to Ron (who is famously difficult); David immediately attacks Tansley for the comparison
jokes.explanation: Good escalating hostility — the fact that these old men immediately return to decades-old grievances is funny, and comparing anyone to Ron as 'worse' is a nice callback to his established character. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, the patient is dead, so... I don't think they'd mind.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I don't mean like, in a creepy way. I just mean like, they're gone, so...

jokes.text: Leslie says 'When I say parks, you say department!' — Clarence yells 'Apartment!'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to get the group energized with a call-and-response chant
jokes.punchline: The oldest man mishears or mishaps the word, responding with 'Apartment!' — which deflates the entire attempt
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical joke about the challenge Leslie faces with these elderly, uncooperative men. 'Apartment' is the right wrong word — close enough to be a plausible mishearing, different enough to be completely useless. Good character beat for both Leslie's optimism and Clarence's haplessness.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Well, he's not dead. He's just sleeping.

jokes.text: Ron: 'I only had one breakfast.'
jokes.setup: Ron is told to relax when he expresses hunger; the group needs to keep moving
jokes.punchline: Ron frames 'one breakfast' as a deprivation — implying he normally has multiple breakfasts and has been genuinely shortchanged
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Ron Swanson jokes. The entire joke is the implication packed into four words: Ron routinely eats multiple breakfasts, considers this normal, and views one breakfast as inadequate. Maximum economy — the joke tells us everything about Ron's appetite, his lifestyle, and his complete unapologetic self-indulgence. Absolutely earns the 8+ score. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Baseball is just the boy version of softball.

jokes.text: Leslie made Ron bacon for a trail snack; Ron already ate it out of her purse and 'could smell it before I even parked my car'
jokes.setup: Leslie reaches into her purse to give Ron the bacon trail snack she prepared
jokes.punchline: Ron already ate it — he smelled it from the parking lot before he even arrived, and now it's gone and 'I hate everything'
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Ron Swanson joke. The escalation is perfect: we learn (1) Leslie made him a snack, (2) he already ate it secretly, (3) he detected bacon through a purse from a parking lot — implying superhuman bacon-sensing ability, (4) he punctuates the confession with 'I hate everything,' redirecting his self-reproach outward. Every beat adds something. Completely earned through character. Fully justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Do we have everything for the picnic?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, we got it all. Well, we did until April threw all the food on the roof.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Why would she do that?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I don't know. I stopped trying to understand April a long time ago.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head four-step plan: nail the photo, book outside gigs, have sex with a model, become a model
jokes.setup: Tom explains his plan for the photo shoot
jokes.punchline: What starts as professional ambition ('nail this photo') escalates through 'have sex with a model' before arriving at the goal of becoming a model himself — with step 3 being completely unrelated to steps 2 and 4
jokes.explanation: Good Tom Haverford list joke — the structure mimics a business plan while burying an absurd personal goal in the middle. Step 3 being 'have sex with a model' sandwiched between legitimate career steps is the key joke. Well-constructed escalation that reveals character.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm sorry I threw the smoked salmon on the roof.

jokes.text: Tom directing the photo shoot: 'Keep slithering! Keep slithering!'
jokes.setup: Tom is directing Ann and Mark in an apparently over-the-top fashion photo shoot
jokes.punchline: 'Keep slithering' as photographic direction — an absurd instruction that implies a snake-like pose being demanded of local government employees
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of 'keep slithering' as a photography direction — implying Tom is running a high-fashion shoot instead of a parks catalog photo — captures his delusion perfectly. The word choice 'slithering' is doing heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Why would you even believe that text was real?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because I wanted to believe it. And when you want to believe something, you'll convince yourself that it's true. It's called being in love, Mark. It's the most romantic thing in the world.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Ann, can you give me something, anything in the face?' / Mark: 'I'm not doing anything, so...'
jokes.setup: Tom is struggling to get Ann to look good in photos while praising Mark
jokes.punchline: Mark reveals he's doing literally nothing — suggesting Ann is being measured against zero effort and still failing by Tom's assessment
jokes.explanation: The joke subverts Tom's fashion-director shtick: Mark is praised for doing nothing, which makes Ann's 'failure' to match him funnier and sets up the later confrontation where Tom tells her face 'isn't working.'

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Tom, there is no such thing as a city-planning emergency.

jokes.text: Clarence explains women shouldn't be in leadership because menstruation directs blood away from the brain
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions her ambition to become the first female parks director
jokes.punchline: Clarence offers a pseudo-scientific explanation rooted in Victorian-era pseudoscience — delivered with complete sincerity and concern for Leslie's 'safety'
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from Clarence's complete sincerity — he's not being malicious, he genuinely believes this and presents it as helpful medical advice. Leslie's silent reaction ('Yeah. Mm-hmm. Sure.') sells it. Dark-ish but positioned as satire of historical attitudes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So Ann and Mark... Ann and Mark... What about 'Marm'? No, that's not good. 'Marl'? 'Nark'? Wait, wait, wait. What about 'Merkins'?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: 'Merkins.' Mark and Ann. Merkins.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: That's not a couple name, that's a thing.

jokes.text: Leslie's silent reaction to Clarence's sexism — cut to her talking head saying only 'No! No!'
jokes.setup: Clarence has just finished explaining why women shouldn't hold leadership roles for their own safety
jokes.punchline: Cut to Leslie in a confessional, producing only two horrified 'No!'s — unable to articulate a fuller response
jokes.explanation: The mockumentary format is perfectly deployed here. Leslie, who is articulate and passionate about women in government, is reduced to a wordless 'No! No!' because there are no words sufficient for what she's just heard. The economy is perfect — two words do more than a paragraph could. A great use of the confessional format.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, I wanted to go on dates with Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm kidding. No, I didn't.

jokes.text: Andy and April spontaneously decide to co-write a picnic song — 'Animal on the head... wait, that's a different song. Life is a picnic...with you.' / 'Then it could be about a girl... or Peyton Manning.'
jokes.setup: Andy wants to write a song about a picnic while at the picnic
jokes.punchline: April enthusiastically adds 'With you' — then Andy suggests the subject could be 'a girl... or Peyton Manning' as equally valid romantic interests
jokes.explanation: Good character beat for both Andy (who wears his man-crushes on athletes openly) and April (who is engaged despite herself). The Peyton Manning pivot is the punchline and captures Andy's earnest weirdness. Light but charming.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, you look terrible. Like, genuinely awful. But I need a huge favor from you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? Tom, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I need you to be in this photo shoot. You're perfect for what I'm going for.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Hey, maybe I should write a song about a picnic.' April: 'Ooh, where'd you come up with that idea?' Andy: 'The picnic we're having.'
jokes.setup: Andy and April are at a picnic; Andy has an idea for a song
jokes.punchline: April's sarcastic question ('Where'd you come up with that idea?') is meant to highlight the obviousness; Andy takes it completely literally and answers earnestly
jokes.explanation: A tight three-line joke with perfect character integration. April's sarcasm is deflected completely by Andy's literal-mindedness — he takes a rhetorical question as genuine curiosity and answers it with total sincerity. The joke could ONLY be this character pairing: April's dry contempt meeting Andy's earnest obliviousness. Economy is near-perfect — 22 words to get the full character dynamic. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Did you guys switch sweaters? Because that one's way too big on you, and that one's way too small on you.

jokes.text: David explains why he took the parks job: 'Clarence was old and weak, so I put in for a transfer, swooped in, and pushed him out.' — No other reason.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks what called David to the parks department — expecting an inspiring origin story
jokes.punchline: He describes predatorily targeting the job by waiting for Clarence to be weak — with zero embarrassment or self-awareness, delivered as a straightforward narrative
jokes.explanation: Excellent subversion of the 'what drew you to public service?' interview format. David's complete absence of civic motivation — replaced with pure Machiavellian opportunism — is presented deadpan, which is funnier than if it were played for villainy. The fact that Clarence is sitting right there makes it better. Strong dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: I thought you were dead.

dialogue.speaker: Clarence
dialogue.line: Dead? I'm not dead. I've been too busy having sex with your wife.

jokes.text: David: 'Who gives a crap about this crap?' — about his entire career in parks
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if there was any other reason David wanted the parks job; he says the actual job is a nightmare
jokes.punchline: He dismisses the entirety of the parks department and his own career as pointless — in front of Leslie, who has devoted her life to it
jokes.explanation: The comedy is the collision between Leslie's passionate devotion and David's complete nihilism about the same job. 'Who gives a crap about this crap?' is a nice turn of phrase. Leslie's implicit off-screen reaction is where the impact lives.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so when I say 'Parks,' you say 'and Rec!' Ready? Parks!

dialogue.speaker: Clarence
dialogue.line: ...Volleyball?

jokes.text: Tom's photo shoot critique: 'Maxim or Good Housekeeping?' — pause — 'I'm not sure which one is the insult.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ann to give more energy in the photo; she doesn't know what direction to take
jokes.punchline: Tom offers two opposite magazines as poles, then admits he doesn't know which is worse — undermining his own authority as a director
jokes.explanation: The self-undermining punchline is the joke — Tom is performing directorial authority but can't maintain the pose when he realizes he doesn't actually know what he means. The two magazines represent opposite ends of the spectrum, which makes his confusion funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm hungry. I normally have three breakfasts by now.

jokes.text: 'Hey, if there's anyone doing a photo shoot about the dangers of eating undercooked chicken, I can give you Ann's phone number.'
jokes.setup: Tom is frustrated with Ann's inability to look good in photos despite being conventionally beautiful
jokes.punchline: He suggests her look is so unhealthy/miserable she'd be perfect as a cautionary image for food poisoning
jokes.explanation: Strong insult joke with great specificity. 'Undercooked chicken' is the key — it's not just 'you look sick,' it's a very particular kind of miserable that paints a vivid picture. The framing ('if there's anyone doing a photo shoot...') adds a layer of dry absurdity. Highly quotable and earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Where did you get this bacon?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I made it this morning. It's just a trail snack.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is the best thing I've ever tasted. I can detect the exact temperature it was cooked at, the breed of pig, and the emotional state of the person who cured it. You're telling me you made this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to have to ask you to make this every day for the rest of my life, or I will die. And it will be your fault.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Bobby, you can have as many juice boxes as you want... Mark, great job. You can have a juice box too. Ann, take a walk with me.'
jokes.setup: Tom pauses the photo shoot to give notes
jokes.punchline: He rewards the child model and Mark with juice boxes as if they're all children, then pulls Ann aside for a talking-to — positioning adult professionals as subjects of Tom's kindergarten-teacher authority
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom joke — the escalating structure (child gets juice, adult gets juice, Ann gets a stern walk) perfectly captures his absurd self-importance. The fact that he casually gives a grown man a juice box as a reward is very funny. The contrast between 'you can have as many as you want' and 'take a walk with me' is well-constructed. Earns the 8.0.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, Ann, Mark—I need you two to slither. Like snakes. Sensual snakes.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Just trust me. Slither toward the camera. Let your bodies undulate with raw, primal energy.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: This is ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no—Mark, you're not committed enough. More slithering! Ann, you're perfect. Keep your eyes locked on mine as you slither.

jokes.text: 'How could someone so hot be so bad at looking hot?'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to coach Ann on being more photogenic
jokes.punchline: He frames her failure as a philosophical paradox — beauty and photogenicity are apparently separate skills she lacks
jokes.explanation: Strong line — the internal paradox ('so hot / so bad at looking hot') is punchy and quotable. Tom's bewilderment is genuine and his framing of it as an unsolvable puzzle is very in character. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mark, you are absolutely killing it. You're a natural. You've got the look, you've got the presence, you've got the cheekbones.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I'm just standing here.

jokes.text: Tom suggests Ann go nude for the photo shoot; Ann says goodbye; Tom: 'I totally understand, but we should get one for safety.'
jokes.setup: Tom has exhausted his options for improving Ann's photos and suggests nudity
jokes.punchline: Ann immediately walks away; Tom pretends to accept this while still requesting 'one for safety' — a film industry term for an extra take, repurposed into something creepy
jokes.explanation: Tom's persistent use of 'one for safety' — a real production term — repurposed after a nudity suggestion is a good detail. His fake reasonableness ('I totally understand') immediately undercut by not backing down at all is true to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Clarence
dialogue.line: Well, you see, the female brain is about 10% smaller than the male brain, which means women are naturally less suited for leadership positions. It's just science.

jokes.text: Tom to Ann about her ring area: 'We need to do something to distract from this ring area.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to get Ann to photograph well and is identifying her alleged photographic problems
jokes.punchline: 'The ring area' — Tom has invented a body-part concern that doesn't exist as a modeling concern — directed at Ann, who is (as the show regularly notes) extremely attractive
jokes.explanation: The made-up modeling problem 'ring area' — combining genuine modeling industry talk with total nonsense — is a good absurdist Tom touch. It sounds real enough to be almost convincing.

dialogue.speaker: Clarence
dialogue.line: You know, I've been reading about the female circulatory system. Women have less blood flow to the brain during their menstrual cycle. It's just science.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not... that's not how that works.

dialogue.speaker: Clarence
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, maybe you should take it easy this week. For your own good. I care about your health.

jokes.text: Clarence: 'If you're menstruating, you'll attract bears.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is leading the group on a hike to the picnic spot
jokes.punchline: Clarence objects to Leslie leading because of a supposed bear-attraction risk from menstruation — delivered as practical safety advice
jokes.explanation: A callback to Clarence's established sexism, escalated to absurdist territory. The bear myth is real (and false), and his confident invocation of it as a leadership disqualifier is very funny. The escalation from 'women shouldn't be in leadership' to 'you'll attract bears' is the joke. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This love song could be about a girl... or Peyton Manning.

jokes.text: 'Holy god.' — Leslie's reaction to Clarence's bear comment
jokes.setup: Clarence tells Leslie she'll attract bears if she leads the hike
jokes.punchline: Leslie's stunned, exhausted 'Holy god' — abandoning her usual diplomatic patience
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Clarence's running sexism: Leslie, who tried to maintain dignity through pseudoscientific blood theories, finally breaks with 'Holy god.' The economy is perfect — two words capture complete exhaustion. The callback structure makes it land harder.

jokes.text: 'Hey! I just whizzed on a butterfly.'
jokes.setup: The group arrives at the picnic spot after a contentious hike
jokes.punchline: Clarence announces with apparent delight that he urinated on a butterfly — completely non-sequitur, cheerfully shared
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. Seven words, completely absurd, delivered mid-arrival at a beautiful picnic. The casual pride in the announcement — 'Hey!' as if sharing good news — is what makes it exceptional. It's unexpected, perfectly timed, and has zero logical setup. The contrast with Leslie's earnest 'it's gonna be good' immediately before it is perfect juxtaposition. Very quotable. Fully earns the high scores.

jokes.text: David: 'You should just copy the Eagleton one. I used to just copy the Eagleton one.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks the former directors for wisdom for her welcome letter
jokes.punchline: David's advice is to plagiarize Pawnee's rival city — which he admits he did routinely throughout his career
jokes.explanation: Good joke that lands on two levels: the anti-civic pride of copying a rival city, and the casual admission of his own laziness. Eagleton as Pawnee's nemesis adds an extra layer for regular viewers. The deadpan revelation ('I used to just copy the Eagleton one') is well-delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, you look terrible. No, worse. Even worse than that. I need you to really lean into looking like you haven't slept in weeks and someone stole your will to live.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm directing. This is what I do now. I'm very good at it.

jokes.text: Old man at picnic: 'I just whizzed on a butterfly.'
jokes.setup: The picnic has just gotten underway after a long, difficult hike; the mood is finally settling
jokes.punchline: Andy's cheerful announcement that he urinated on a butterfly — delivered with the tone of someone reporting good news
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The perfect storm of unexpected content ('whizzed on a butterfly'), extreme economy (five words), tonal incongruity (cheerful delivery), and high quotability. 'I just whizzed on a butterfly' has a rhythm that makes it immediately memorable. The word 'whizzed' rather than any other synonym is a deliberate, perfect choice. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, you look like a young Meryl Streep mixed with a young Grace Jones.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Those are both compliments?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, not really. One's a bit cold, and the other one scares people.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So both comparisons are insulting?

jokes.text: Michael's marijuana legalization argument: 'Thomas Jefferson grew hemp. Alcohol is legal, but pot isn't? That makes sense to you, Ron?' / Ron: 'I'm sorry. I can't hear hippies.'
jokes.setup: Michael makes a reasoned argument for marijuana legalization at the picnic
jokes.punchline: Ron dismisses the entire argument not by countering it but by categorizing the speaker as a 'hippie' — rendering him literally inaudible
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Ron Swanson line. 'I can't hear hippies' is perfect — it's not that he disagrees with the argument, it's that the category of speaker renders the words physically inaudible to him. It's completely Ron: ideological, uncompromising, and delivered as a simple factual statement. The economy is near-perfect. Highly quotable. Fully earns the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, you looked great out there. Really great. I mean, for someone who has the natural charisma of a filing cabinet and the stage presence of a potted plant.

jokes.text: April: if she had to sleep with one of the old men, it would be Clarence because she's 'an eyebrow girl' and wants to 'chew his eyebrows off'
jokes.setup: Someone asks April which old man she'd sleep with
jokes.punchline: April, with total sincerity, explains her preference is based on eyebrow attraction — and her goal would be to consume them
jokes.explanation: Very strong April joke. The escalation from 'the super old one' to 'I'm an eyebrow girl' to 'I want to make out with him and chew his eyebrows off' is perfectly April — each step more specific and more disturbing. The earnestness ('I'm an eyebrow girl' as a statement of aesthetic preference) is what makes it great rather than just gross. Character-specific and highly original.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? Let's just photoshop Leslie's head onto a more attractive body.

jokes.text: Ron's mocking old-man impression: 'Oh, I want water. I'm so old. I need to drink water.'
jokes.setup: One of the old directors asks for water
jokes.punchline: Ron mocks the request with an exaggerated impression, apparently speaking about Clarence behind his face
jokes.explanation: Ron doing a mocking impression is slightly out of character (he's usually more stoic in his disdain), but it's still funny and gets the job done. The impression itself is mild — 'I need to drink water' isn't especially cutting. Functional but not distinguished.

dialogue.speaker: Clarence
dialogue.line: You shouldn't lead us to the picnic. Bears can smell the menstruation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? That's not true.

dialogue.speaker: Clarence
dialogue.line: Well that's what I read on the bear community website.

jokes.text: Clarence: 'I don't need your help, jailbird.'
jokes.setup: Ron is mocking Clarence; someone defends or intervenes
jokes.punchline: Clarence calls Ron a 'jailbird' — implying Ron has a criminal history that was never previously established
jokes.explanation: The word 'jailbird' implies Ron has been arrested at some point, which is a funny unconfirmed detail that enriches his character. The casual escalation of insults between these old men maintains the running gag of their hostility. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: David: 'If there's any unclaimed meat or cheese, I would like to claim it.' — pausing the argument to address food
jokes.setup: The old men are mid-argument about job succession
jokes.punchline: David interrupts the hostilities to calmly lay claim to unclaimed charcuterie — as if both things are equally important
jokes.explanation: Great deadpan beat — David's priorities are completely clear. The formality of 'I would like to claim it' applied to snack food is the joke. Good economy and character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You were on parole.

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: Yes, okay, fine. I was on parole. And yes, I may have used drugs. Constantly. But that's not the point.

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: The point is, drugs should be legal. All of them. We're criminalizing a plant that grows out of the ground. That the government put there. To test us.

jokes.text: Michael reveals he has planted marijuana in community gardens all over the city
jokes.setup: Michael has been advocating for marijuana legalization; his argument was that it grows in the ground
jokes.punchline: He reveals he's been acting on this belief by planting weed across Pawnee's public spaces — and claims it hasn't hurt anyone
jokes.explanation: Strong escalation joke — Michael's abstract marijuana advocacy suddenly becomes very concrete criminal activity at a community level. The casual delivery and 'it hasn't hurt anyone' defense is very funny. Works as a dark punchline on his earlier speeches and adds a great detail to the Pawnee mythology.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no strong feelings one way or the other about marijuana legalization. But I do have strong feelings about hippies, and it's that they should all be eliminated.

jokes.text: Ron: 'You are one pot-loving motherpain in the rectum.'
jokes.setup: Michael has revealed his city-wide marijuana planting; Ron is exasperated
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers what would be a profane insult but self-censors mid-word ('mother-pain') in a way that is somehow more Ron than just swearing
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron joke. The self-censored profanity — 'motherpain in the rectum' — is funnier than the uncensored version would be, because it reveals Ron's commitment to a certain standard of decorum even in maximum irritation. 'In the rectum' as a medical euphemism appended to a near-swear is very Ron. The character integration is near-perfect. Fully earns the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'd need to see their eyebrows first. I have very specific tastes. They need to be thick, dark, and most importantly, edible. I want to consume them slowly while they sleep.

jokes.text: Leslie threatens to shove Clarence's face into the brambles; turns to Ron: 'You're next, buddy.'
jokes.setup: Clarence makes another menstruation comment; Leslie has reached her limit
jokes.punchline: Leslie delivers a specific physical threat then pivots immediately to threaten Ron — showing she's equally done with him
jokes.explanation: Great Leslie moment — her usual diplomacy completely abandoned, revealing the fury underneath. The pivot to Ron ('You're next, buddy') catches him off guard and implies she has a running list of grievances. The physical specificity of 'those brambles' is a nice detail. Character payoff on a long running gag.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why are you asking me for water? You're not elderly enough yet.

jokes.text: Andy directs the old men for a group photo: 'Come on, get out of your seat, turds.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Andy to take a photo of the group
jokes.punchline: Andy addresses the elderly former civic leaders as 'turds' with complete cheerfulness
jokes.explanation: Pure Andy — he has no filter, no concept of respect for authority, and deploys 'turds' as an entirely friendly address. The word is mild enough to be charming rather than offensive, and it's completely in character. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: I got that job the same way I got this baked potato at the airport: I saw it, I wanted it, and I took it.
That's not how you acquire things.

dialogue.speaker: David
dialogue.line: It's worked for me so far.

jokes.text: Tom: 'I tried to photoshop it to make it look like they were happy. It was really hard. Their mouths are just so old.'
jokes.setup: The team reviews the picnic photos; Tom has attempted to improve them
jokes.punchline: His excuse for failing: 'Their mouths are just so old' — as if elderly mouths are a technical photoshop obstacle rather than an expression problem
jokes.explanation: Great specific detail — 'their mouths are just so old' as a photoshop challenge is an unusual and very funny framing. It treats aging as a technical problem Tom faces rather than a human quality. Good character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: Look, I'm just saying, if we legalize marijuana, think about all the tax revenue. It's a win-win.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Michael, that's... actually not a terrible point.

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: Right? I've been doing my own research. You know, for a long time now. Very hands-on research. I have like eight plants in my apartment right now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what?

dialogue.speaker: Michael
dialogue.line: What? I thought we were having a hypothetical conversation!

jokes.text: April shows the 'obstruction series' and 'the future' photo — a completely blurry image — as serious artistic options for the catalog
jokes.setup: The team is reviewing options for the catalog cover
jokes.punchline: April presents a blurry photo called 'the future' with complete artistic seriousness; when Ann points out it's blurry, April simply: 'Yes it is, Ann.'
jokes.explanation: Callback to April's earlier pretentious photo pitch, but escalated — now she's naming blurry photos. 'Yes it is, Ann' as a response to 'it's completely blurry' — confirming the flaw as if it's beside the point — is perfectly deadpan April. The economy of that response is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Clarence
dialogue.line: Can we do one where we're all making funny faces?

jokes.text: April presents the 'Ann and Mark swing photos' — Tom calls them the 'unhappy wife photos'
jokes.setup: The team reviews the supposedly normal photos of Ann and Mark on a swing
jokes.punchline: Tom has already categorized and filed them as 'unhappy wife photos' — implying this is an established genre he regularly encounters
jokes.explanation: Tom's naming of the photo subcategory is the joke — the implication that 'unhappy wife photos' is a known type he files mentally. The efficiency of the label is very funny and Ann's reaction ('I look miserable / You do look kind of miserable') confirms it accurately.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm trying to Photoshop these old men to look happy, but it's really hard because their mouths are so ancient and rigid. I think I'm just going to have to draw new mouths on them.

jokes.text: 'Now you know what I meant by make your face better.'
jokes.setup: Ann acknowledges she looked miserable in the photos
jokes.punchline: Tom uses this as vindication for his earlier direction 'make your face better' — an absurd thing to say that now seems retrospectively reasonable
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Tom's indefensible earlier direction ('make your face better') is retroactively justified by the evidence, which is funny because the advice is still terrible regardless. His vindication is completely unearned yet logically coherent.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This one is called 'The Future.' It's blurry, which represents the uncertainty of what's to come.

jokes.text: Tom calls the photos of Ann and Mark on the swing 'the unhappy wife photos'; Leslie immediately agrees that Ann looks miserable.
jokes.setup: The team is reviewing the swing photos that were supposed to be the 'normal' catalog shot
jokes.punchline: Tom's label 'unhappy wife photos' is instantly confirmed by everyone — including Ann herself — making it a moment of accidental truth and mild Ann self-awareness
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the entire photo shoot subplot — Ann's inability to look happy — confirmed by a photo of her on a swing looking genuinely miserable. The 'unhappy wife' framing adds a relationship dimension (is she unhappy WITH Mark?). Good subplot closer.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What about these normal swing photos?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Those are my 'unhappy wife' photos.

jokes.text: Leslie's welcome letter is blank — she printed a blank piece of paper
jokes.setup: Leslie reads Ron what she has for her welcome letter so far, saying 'nothing' — Ron heard the printer going
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals she printed a blank piece of paper — she literally produced nothing, materialized as paper
jokes.explanation: Clean visual/structural joke — the printer noise set up an expectation of something, and it's undercut by the blank page. Ron's delivery ('Oh, wisdom — finally') is the perfect button, treating blankness as a relief from the day's noise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is a disgusting fragrance flap.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Oh, wisdom — finally.' — responding to the blank piece of paper
jokes.setup: Leslie reveals her welcome letter is blank; Ron sees the paper
jokes.punchline: Ron greets the blank page as 'wisdom — finally' — treating the absence of content as the most insightful thing produced all day
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Ron Swanson line. Three words summarize Ron's entire worldview: he has endured a day of noise, bad advice, and conflict, and greets a blank page as the most useful thing produced. It's also a completely accurate assessment of the day. Perfect character integration — only Ron would say this. Maximum economy. Earns the 8+ score comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't need a fake ID. I rely on confidence. Confidence and a very convincing story about how I left my wallet at home.

jokes.text: Leslie replacing the welcome letter with the 'Yearning' fragrance ad: 'Good-bye, distilled wisdom of 50 years of experience. Hello, disgusting fragrance flap.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has failed to get any usable wisdom from the former directors; she decides to use the fragrance ad instead
jokes.punchline: She formally eulogizes the wisdom she never got while cheerfully welcoming something she clearly finds gross — the comedy is in the formal structure she gives to a completely deflating moment
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie line — the ceremonial structure she gives to failure is very her. 'Disgusting fragrance flap' is a very specific and funny phrase. The acceptance of defeat wrapped in formal language is Leslie at her most endearing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So wait, you're saying that every Parks director before me left on bad terms with the one after them?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's correct.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, that's not going to happen with us, right? I mean, we're friends. We'll always be friends.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We'll see.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'we'll see'? Ron, you're scaring me.

jokes.text: Ron accidentally takes a personal/embarrassing photo when looking for the picnic photo; Leslie calls it 'the wrong one' but admits the 'real one's very bad as well.'
jokes.setup: Leslie needs the group photo from the picnic
jokes.punchline: Ron produces an inappropriate personal photo by mistake, and Leslie's concession that the actual picnic photo is 'very bad as well' confirms the entire day was a disaster on record
jokes.explanation: A mild callback beat. Mainly confirms the day's total failure rather than generating a new joke, but Leslie's weary 'the real one's very bad as well' is a good deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron said he wants to be city manager so he can dismantle the government from the inside. Well, I want to be city manager so I can build it up, make it better, expand it. And unlike Ron, I'm actually going to win.

jokes.text: Andy and April attempting to get into a bar — April's ID says she's 20; she claims to be 24, then 25
jokes.setup: Andy and April decide to get a drink after the picnic and go to a bar
jokes.punchline: April's ID reveals she's 20; she tries claiming to be 24, then 25 when caught — the bouncer is unimpressed
jokes.explanation: The scene works because of what it reveals: April, who presents herself as so cool and beyond caring, is undone by something as simple as being 20. The bouncer's 'No old jokes, please' is a nice detail. Character revelation comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Some people want to enjoy their life.

jokes.text: Bouncer: 'You're not even gonna show me a fake?' / April: 'Sometimes the confidence confuses people.'
jokes.setup: April's real ID shows she's 20; she doesn't have a fake
jokes.punchline: April explains her strategy — pure confidence as a substitute for documentation — and the bouncer is grudgingly impressed by it as a technique
jokes.explanation: Excellent April line. 'Sometimes the confidence confuses people' is a perfectly constructed explanation of a completely absurd strategy — and it reveals something true about April's general approach to life. The bouncer's 'You're good, bro' response as grudging admiration makes it better. Maximum character integration, very quotable. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Michael made a bong out of a stuffed raccoon. Right here in this office.

jokes.text: After being denied entry, April awkwardly offers to take Andy to another bar that 'always lets me in' — followed by mutual fumbled excuses to leave separately.
jokes.setup: Andy and April can't get into the bar; April offers an alternative and begins to suggest they go together
jokes.punchline: Both characters simultaneously retreat into excuses ('I should be going home... clean and stuff'), revealing they both want to go but neither will admit it — followed by increasingly awkward goodbyes
jokes.explanation: This is primarily a character/romance beat rather than a pure joke, but the comedy of mutual awkward retreat — 'I should go home... clean and stuff' — is effective cringe. For viewers who know where Andy and April end up, this is a rich rewatch moment. The comedy is in the painful mutual awareness and denial. Parks & Rec at its best uses cringe to do emotional work simultaneously.

jokes.text: Ron and Leslie's bar — 'The usual, Marta' — they have regulars at a diner that serves breakfast at night
jokes.setup: After the disastrous day, Ron and Leslie go somewhere to decompress
jokes.punchline: Both order 'the usual' at what is apparently a diner they frequent — establishing that their friendship includes regular late-night breakfast visits, which is very them
jokes.explanation: More of a warm character beat than a pure joke, but the simultaneous 'the usual, Marta' establishes their friendship in a funny, economical way. Works better as character texture than as a comedy moment.

jokes.text: 'I really made love to the pooch on this one.' / Ron: 'Screwed the pooch?' / Leslie: 'I don't like that term. It's so vulgar.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is expressing regret about the disastrous day
jokes.punchline: She uses a sanitized malapropism of 'screwed the pooch' — 'made love to the pooch' — which is somehow more disturbing; when Ron corrects her, she objects to the original as 'vulgar' despite her version being worse
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among the best Leslie Knope character moments. The comedy works on multiple levels: (1) she accidentally made a cleaner phrase more disturbing, (2) she objects to the original on grounds of vulgarity without recognizing her version is worse, (3) it's completely in character — Leslie is always improving things that don't need improving and making them inadvertently worse. Near-perfect character integration. The economy is excellent. Very quotable. Approaches the 9.5 anchor calibration. One of the strongest jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Ron's impression of what Leslie wanted the old directors to say: 'Leslie, you are the next link in a wonderful chain... you are the chosen one.'
jokes.setup: Leslie explains what went wrong — she expected wisdom and validation from the former directors
jokes.punchline: Ron articulates her fantasy in increasingly grandiose terms, ending on 'you are the chosen one' — gently mocking her idealism
jokes.explanation: Good Ron moment — he's perceptive enough to articulate exactly what Leslie wanted but too honest to let it go unexamined. 'You are the chosen one' as the apex of her fantasy is a nice escalating punchline. Warm rather than cruel.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Are we gonna hate each other someday?' / Ron: 'I don't think so. I think we're gonna be fine.'
jokes.setup: Leslie worries because every former director hated their job and everyone they worked with
jokes.punchline: Ron's response — 'I don't think so. I think we're gonna be fine.' — is understated reassurance from a man who expresses almost no positive emotion
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the character context: Ron Swanson saying 'I think we're gonna be fine' is an enormous emotional statement for him, delivered with his usual flat affect. It's funny because of how much it understates what is actually a genuine moment of warmth. For regular viewers, this lands hard.

jokes.text: Ron talks-head: 'When I become city manager, my first act will be to propose eliminating the parks department, although I expect a spirited debate with Leslie.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just told Leslie he's not going to stab her in the back
jokes.punchline: His confessional immediately reveals his actual ambition — to eliminate her entire department, though he concedes she'll put up a fight
jokes.explanation: Classic mockumentary structural joke — the talking head immediately undercuts what was just said in the scene. Ron's plan to eliminate Leslie's department is perfectly in character (he believes government should be smaller) and his acknowledgment that she'd fight him adds a layer of genuine mutual respect. The deadpan delivery implied makes this land well. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Leslie's counter talking-head: 'I'll win.' — after detailing her plan to double the parks department
jokes.setup: Leslie mirrors Ron's talking head with her own ambition — becoming city manager and doubling the parks department
jokes.punchline: After predicting Ron will fight her, she simply concludes 'But I'll win' — with total certainty
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback and excellent Leslie character moment. The parallel structure of the two confessionals (Ron says she'll fight him, Leslie says she'll win) is elegant. Two words — 'But I'll win' — delivered as pure fact, not bravado. The economy is perfect. The confidence is completely Leslie. Earns the 8+.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Oh, why would anybody ever eat anything besides breakfast food?' / Leslie: 'People are idiots, Leslie.'
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie are eating at the diner; food has arrived
jokes.punchline: Ron poses what he clearly considers a genuine philosophical question about meal structure; Leslie validates it by agreeing 'people are idiots' — creating a mutual bubble of breakfast supremacy
jokes.explanation: Excellent double-character joke. Ron's passionate belief in breakfast food is perfectly established; Leslie confirming 'people are idiots, Leslie' (calling herself 'Leslie' as a collective address, or perhaps momentarily forgetting who she's talking to) is wonderfully absurd and warm. The shared enthusiasm creates a perfect window into their friendship. Very quotable. Earns the 8.0.

jokes.text: Leslie's welcome letter conclusion: 'they taught me a valuable lesson — there's nothing more important than friendship'
jokes.setup: The catalog arrives; Leslie reads her welcome letter aloud, which describes the day with the horrible old directors
jokes.punchline: She concludes that a day with awful, sexist, hostile men who gave her nothing taught her that 'friendship' is most important — a lesson she invented entirely from disappointment
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie joke — her ability to extract a wholesome lesson from a completely miserable experience is quintessential Leslie Knope. The gap between the terrible day and the cheerful conclusion is the comedy. Ron's 'It's a little flowery' / 'Shut up' exchange is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Ron reveals Michael made a water pipe out of a stuffed raccoon — 'He made a bong out of a taxidermied raccoon'
jokes.setup: Ron and Clarence are reflecting warmly on Michael's skills after the terrible day
jokes.punchline: Michael's impressive 'water-pipe-making skills' turn out to be literal drug paraphernalia — specifically from a taxidermied raccoon, calling back to the raccoon hat from the cold open
jokes.explanation: Outstanding closing joke. It works as a triple payoff: (1) callback to the raccoon hat cold open (which now gains a new context — raccoons and this show), (2) payoff on Michael's marijuana subplot, and (3) pure absurdist comedy of a bong made from a taxidermied animal. The structure — building from 'water-pipe-making skills' to the reveal — is excellently constructed. Ron reporting this with apparent admiration is perfect. Among the episode's best moments.

jokes.text: 'Right in Clarence's ancient junk.' — during a food fight at the end
jokes.setup: A food fight apparently breaks out at the end of the picnic; someone scores a hit
jokes.punchline: The hit lands in Clarence's groin — 'ancient junk' is the descriptor
jokes.explanation: Functional slapstick closer — the phrase 'ancient junk' is the elevated element that makes a groin-hit joke slightly more interesting than generic. The visual implied (a very old man getting hit there) adds to it. Not crafted, but lands with physical comedy energy as an ending.

tmdb_overview: Preparing the Summer Events Catalog, Leslie decides to take Ron and the past directors of the Parks Department out for a picnic lunch. Tom enlists the help of Ann and Mark to pose for the cover photo.
insight: Summer catalog logistics anchor 70 jokes, but midseason slump shows in modest 72.1 index.
